target_customer: Busy individuals and, later, businesses that pay a subscription or per-task fee for human virtual assistants
problem: People and small companies have long task lists and little time, and want to hand off errands and admin work through a simple text or chat interface.
business_model: Subscription and usage-based virtual assistant service staffed by human assistants (SMS concierge at launch, later B2B executive, admin and sales support)

founders.name: Mike Chen
founders.background_notes: YC page lists no background. A search result snippet says Chen and Kemmer previously built Made In Space, not verified on an opened page.

founders.name: Aaron Kemmer
founders.role: Founder; CEO 2023 to 2026 per YC page
previous_startups: Made In Space (founding CEO, per YC page)
founders.background_notes: YC page says ARR grew from 3M to 40M during his CEO tenure and that he is now Executive Chairman of Edge Aerospace.

founders.name: David Merriman
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page with no background.

founders.name: Nic Novak
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page with no background.

founders.name: Michael Rubin
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page with no background.

competitors.name: Zirtual
competitors.traction_then: Venture-funded virtual assistant startup; abruptly laid off its assistants in August 2015
competitors.funding_then: raised millions in venture funding per the cited coverage

technical_complexity.rationale: At launch the service was an SMS short code in front of human assistants, a weekend project per press, so the hard part was operations and hiring rather than software.

defensibility.rationale: Human labor behind a text interface was easy to copy; a July 2015 post says copycats and niche variants appeared quickly after Magic went viral.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No large incumbent bought or copied it. Copycat startups appeared in 2015 and Zirtual collapsed in August 2015, while Magic pivoted toward B2B assistants and survived.

market_need_then: Strong early curiosity: coverage says 17,000 text messages arrived in the first 48 hours and the launch trended on Product Hunt and Hacker News. Sustained willingness to pay at consumer scale was less proven.

branding.name_origin: Company materials say the founders wanted a service that handles everything with one text message, like magic.
branding.domain_note: Operates at getmagic.com, so a prefix domain rather than exact magic.com; acquisition history not found.

identity.voice_and_tone: Confident, upbeat and conversational, with casual assistant messages and emojis on the site.

branding.brand_signature: A single text number (short code) that does anything for you
branding.community_and_virality: Went viral on Product Hunt and Hacker News within two weeks of the 2015 launch per press and a Hacker News thread.

brand_strength.rationale: The name is memorable and the launch was viral, but it collides with many other companies called Magic and no source shows lasting brand pull.

outcome_analysis: Magic launched a viral SMS concierge in 2015 and raised a Sequoia led Series A reported at 12M, then survived while rival Zirtual collapsed. It is still active with about 350 staff, and the YC page says ARR grew from 3M to 40M during 2023 to 2026 under Aaron Kemmer as CEO. The path was a move from consumer errands toward B2B assistant outsourcing.
notes: The Sequoia round is reported by TechCrunch as 'raising' from sources; a $40M valuation is reported but whether pre or post money is unclear, so post_money is null. An aggregator lists 39.1M total across three rounds, unverified. SV Angel and Slow Ventures are reported as participants in a search summary, not verified. A $320M 'Magic AI' Series C in results belongs to a different company. The 2023 to 2026 CEO claim comes from the YC page only. Competitor Zirtual's source is dated August 2015, about five months after the batch. Fancy Hands (founded 2010 per undated pages) is omitted because no dated source was found.
